On the example video it detects takeoff at frame 53 and landing at frame 62, and it writes `/app/output.toml`. I only had the one example video, so I haven't tested it on others.\n\n```toml\njump_takeoff_frame_number = 53\njump_land_frame_number = 62\n```\n\n**How it works:**\n1. It treats the first frame as an empty background and finds the athlete in each frame by differencing against it, with some blur and noise cleanup.\n2. It ignores frames where the athlete is entering or leaving the image, because the bounding box is cut off there.\n3. It tracks the lowest point of the athlete, which is roughly the feet. While the athlete is on the ground this stays near the ground line. In the air it rises.\n4. It finds the run of frames around the peak where the lowest point is clearly above the ground line, which is the airborne phase. Takeoff is the frame just before it and landing is the frame just after it.\n\n**Checks on the example:** I looked at montages of frames 40–75. The athlete's foot is still on the ground at 53, the feet are clearly up and over the hurdle by 54–61, and the foot is back down at 62.\n\n**Things to know:**\n- The `toml` module isn't installed in this environment, so the script uses it if present and otherwise writes the two lines by hand. The output is the same either way.\n- The \"clearly above the ground\" threshold is 16 px, which I tuned on the one example video. A different athlete or jump style might need it adjusted.\n- With no arguments the script reads `/app/example_video.mp4` and writes `/app/output.toml`. You can instead run `python jump_analyzer.py video.mp4 [out.toml]`.","time":{"start":1793303810840,"end":1793303810840}}}
